So here's what we look for on the charts:

General: HTF. Know where price is coming from and going to, and the PA past and present in all the TFs, from the Monthly down.

Specific: At the zones you want to trade, look to

Past. study the zone in all TFs, down to M1 ask yourself Where were the decisions made? Clean S/D? Mark these lines. No clean S/D? -compressed zone Did price really shoot away form the zone, or did it cp away? Did the zone itself react at the right place? Look beyond the zone further into the past. See what it reacted to. Was there a better S/D nearby that price wants to visit? This explains many fakeouts.

Present. Approach. How is price returning to the zone? Where's the nearest flag in the TF you want to trade? This is your tg1 in this TF. Flags in the LTFs? What does PA tell you? Has price tested the last flag on approach? (good sign) Has price compressed into the zone in this TF or LTFs? (good sign) Is there big news on the way? Has there just been big news?

Reaction In LTF, does price react violently to the first decision point? Does it quickly engulf the nearest S/D? (good sign) Does price simply CP away? Maybe it wants to go to the next decision point If the first decision point breaks, watch the signs on approach to the next, and, of course, reaction.

Chew this over for now. Apply it to your chart history. Apply it to as many failed setups as successful ones. Millions of them if possible! Capture and file them all. This will help make it instinctive

You have a good eye and good analysis. As I tell most people, the first part of analysis is being anal, and your attention to detail is good. I will add on a few observations for you.

Above your first compression zone where the C letter is located you have two areas in blue boxes for buying. Technically correct, but dont loose sight of the higher time frames and where the current time frame is, and in this instance the Euro is winding down and the two buying areas wont have the same effect, they will very get blown through. The major selling areas higher up the chart tell you the story.

Compare the other compression zones and the effect of buyers had on the price when it came back down to test them. Virtually all of them provide little impact.

There are times when price runs off quickly such as prior to your 2nd last compression zone, the 2nd compression zone slowly down price and also setup a move back up to collect more sellers where you see your 2 decision areas way over on the left. This also was a resistance area of significance. Those deep pull backs are probably among the most difficult part of trading, in that they throw you for a loop until you can see where the next most obvious resistance is for a continued down move.

Good work!

Every DBR and RBD has its own importance and value, and nearly every one can be traded. For each one that you find, zoom out to the HTFs, and see what historical significance the decision point has. Perhaps it's a failure to get back into an important PA Zone - these ones are special. justinforex wrote: Question - A Valid RBD

It does not have to break the previous H/L to become a valid base.

What defines a base it that price moves up or down, bases (consolidates, congests, clusters, ect) then moves again either up or down.

Here are the variations. The standard DBD and RBR then the RBR and DBD then RBD during downtrend and DBR during uptrend.

Hopefully this could give you a better understanding. However as you have alluded to, H/L or S/R levels are almost always an intrinsic part to the development of any base. If you can find the levels responsible for the bases it can give you a much holistic picture on the chart.

The two charts on the right, in HTF, can often look just like the two charts on the left. It's worth looking into these on your charts, and finding out which tend to perform better on price return - drop/consolidation/drops or drop/RBD/Drops, and the same for rallies

I'll present to you the way I would do the analysis. It is probably not the only way and certainly not the only 'correct' way but it seems to have been working for me so far.

The first chart is the daily and you can see that price has gone into daily demand, so you are looking for buying opportunities. But beware, though, it is not a fresh demand zone.

In the 4H chart you can see a couple of D/S zones, so you might think: "hmmm, maybe price could move to the upside to at least retest those zones". However, as I said, daily demand is not fresh so price might need to go lower in order to move higher and take them out... PA will let us know.

As you can see on the 1H charts, price has reached a 1H demand level within daily demand. Now this 1H demand zone is fresh and it was reached after price generated a 1H supply zone just above the demand zone. Therefore, I am looking for buying opportunities into the next supply zone.

So we can conclude that price is in an important zone. That's where PA really matters. That's where you must pay attention to PA. If you check out the following link

So after being one of the first members of Ace, I have finally started my homework assignments. Time to start going up the ladder. feedback from anyone is helping. A quick thanks to Redknight for coming up with a great format for marking the charts, helps you keep count of the zones and how succesful they are.

Here are my learning from doing the homework, 1 - scroll slowly through the charts, so that the new candle come up slowly and you can "paper trade". Identify your zones without seeing the reaction, this is key to helping you understand the zones and how they work, and that zones seem to fail at first.

2. read through other peoples homework and get an understanding. In school this was called copying, in this business it's called "benchmarking" and highly encouraged. 3. After a while you will close your eyes and see charts!

Here is how to read my notes on my charts. U = untested on this screen R = reaction (normally first) B/E = breakeven, i.e. price reacts, but then goes through the level (decision point) often time you may be able to move your theoritical stop loss to breakeven Ig = ignored (at first)

Just some lessons I have learnt from this exercise. Hi madwt,

This is my take on how new demand/supply levels are created.

Fresh zone are created from an old zone of the opposing type. By that I mean, what was old demand can become fresh supply when price creates a flip zone.

On the chart posted lets assume for the purpose of this example that the left hand side of the chart is a price flip zone which means it was previous supply.

When price broke thru at (1) it cleared out all the supply so only demand was left at that level. We don't know how strong this is (although how price went thru the level and how far it travelled gives us a clue). There was an initial retest of this level a few bars later which showed there was still plenty of demand.

Price came back again at (2) and this is now considered old demand but it was still good enough to hold price again.

At point (3) there was a little reaction up consuming the remaining buy orders and so demand was all used up and price fell thru creating a new supply zone at that level. Price moved well below the level quite strongly so we can determine this is a good level to short next time back.

Point (4) is the first time back to the new supply level so a good place to short. That level is now considered to be old supply.

We don't know if a level will hold or how many times a level will hold so we look to the chart for clues.

Hope this explanation is clear enough to follow.

Take aways from looking at the DBR and RBD's:

1. When price moves away from a level, it doesnt matter how soon a re-test back into that comes, thats the highest probability trade because of the probability of unfilled orders resting there.

2. When price rallies back into a previous RBD, the supply that came from the D of that previous RBD was cause of a new area of supply to form that is slightly lower than the previous (often). This causes the lower market structure highs to form, because new levels of supply just below the previous market structure highs has formed, capping price from reaching higher levels. This works both ways, and is what seems to happen many times, not always.

3. Price seems clearer to me that it is always moving around to find piles of orders, and depending on the strength of moves away from those piles, we can reason better about what the probabilities are when price revisits and retests.

4. Wicks or tails mean at the point price reached that extent, there were S/D pushing price faster than the opposing direction, but then that move is overwhelmed by the orders that get touched and filled.

5. When resting orders sit at these levels, they only execute when market orders take them out, or other execution mechanics force those orders to move to market orders. It is still liquidity takers that must drive price through these levels.

6. When price breaks out of a recent high or base, it often returns on the other side and re-tests. Re-testing suggests a conscious act for price to go test a previous level. To me it seems like it is more a result of price bouncing away from supply and working its way back to value, but as it hits the demand that was strong enough to break those highs, thats were orders exist to give this level support. This is S/R in action.

Hello tradingjedi,

As well as identifying the RBDs and DBRs, you need to mark out at what level reactions occurred (if any), consider those that failed and what happened at the level afterwards. Maybe not to the same degree that mettafort and I have just done - we had a common interest but different perspectives to explore, hopefully to the benefit of everyone.

A long while back I was in a webinar and the speaker made an almost throw-away statement - which I'm sure sailed straight through most people, but which piqued my interest. It was in response to a question I don't recall, but the reply was, "Although we look at the same charts, we see different things". There was more to it than that, but pondering that statement allowed me to form many questions I didn't even know I needed to ask, then answer them to find more questions. It started me on a path of discoveries - still ongoing - that I doubt I would've walked otherwise. I won't expand beyond that, but what is interesting is that three people looked at roughly the same GBPUSD information and applied their logic to it: two of those people had entirely different opinions of the same RBD and one person ignored it altogether on their chart!

So, the benefit comes from the qualitative exercise:

1. What attracted you to this particular RBD or DBR?, what didn't you like? Was your opinion that it would work or not? (Your opinion, mind, not the benefit of 20:20 hindsight 2. What happened when price did return to the Base in each case? If it reacted, where (zoom in to the Base and root around)? If it didn't, is there anything that you can learn about it so you can spot a bad-un in the future (that's why we need to find good and bad examples)?

3. What happened later when price returned to the Base from the other side? Did it react or ignore it again? 4. Zoom out and look back in time, does that change your perception of your chosen examples or help understand why some worked or failed?

By going through this process on your charts you will better train your brain to spot and sort these patterns out, and assess the likely turning point within them so you can successfully reduce your exposure in the market (by this I'm sort of referring to R:R, but I'm also taking time into account). And if you keep hitting a wall in your understanding it will better help everyone else to offer suggestions or guidance.

You don't need to slap everything on the chart, just your main line of reasoning and points of interest, maybe a little bit of filler in the post, but in doing so you will accelerate your understanding.

BTW, why didn't you mark up that RBD?:)

Regards.

Spongy.

Hiya Bravo,

The exercise is to identify working and failing RBDs and DBRs, to analyse them on different time-frames, then to watch what happens at those levels in the future, even after they fail. The idea is - by repetition - to get your brain to recognise attributes of each so you can hone your skills to spot their viability in real time, and choose prospective turning points within.

I do this by asking a series of questions to get me to really look at them, and I refine my questions and observations with each pass. I'm not saying my way is the right way or that I even ask the right questions, just that they cause me to take a good look, and think. Hopefully a pattern database is being built somewhere in the dark recesses of my mind as a result.

I wouldn't go so far as to say every peak or trough is RBD or DBR (that's my point of view and I might be entirely wrong, but a spike doesn't necessarily have a base on a shorter time-frame): they can certainly be caps on price, analysis would determine whether they are Supply, Demand or reaction.

Hope this helps.

Spongy.

Nothing promises that zone will hold price, even at first visit. The zones we mark on the charts are mainly a mapping of decisions in the market. Decision can take price either way. Zones are meant to be broken, and this market decision has its own significance too.

As further you go with your reading skills, you will be able read the hints and clues for zones to hold or to break. Your task at this time, is to train your eyes defining the zones.

Your next step, is to investigate how price is behaving around these zones. there are few things you should bare in mind while you do this work: 1. Be aware of how price had printed the zone you marked, what it was reacting to, and how the decision of price to move further look like. 2. Be aware of how price is approaching the Zones, what is the dynamic. 3. Is price come from a valid opposite zone? Remember that price goes from Demand to Supply and vice versa. 4. Be aware of the reaction of the first touch, how deep it went inside, what had stopped it if any? 5. what are higher or lower TF tell you. SD discipline is a Multi time frame concept. We trade price levels, not candles, so Story may vary on different TF 6. (more Advanced) Look for correlations with Index and other pairs.

it might look intimidating, but actually it's should be very simple. Zones are always a reaction of past Price Action (aka: always look left). As much as you can go back in history, the better your understand be of how price move. there is no randomness for this market, all can be explained with PA reaction, result, decision. just look for reasoning for levels and zones creation.

Best,

Probably simpler just to have one at the low of the zone (that DP) unless the zone is a particularly wide one.

3b. The reaction has a couple of good, strong bear engulfs, and a nice rejection after these.

7a: RBD

This is interesting, as it shows why moving your stop to BE is a bad idea, and can take you out of a winning trade, especially if you go short at 7b, the retest of the DP to break the highs of the RBD (this will be a flag on a LTF). The drop from the high of 7a made a decent engulf, so a target at least back down to that engulf, around 'x' would be reasonable. That's only about a 1:1 RRR, though.

What I'm learning is that now the DP has been tested, we should watch for shorting opportunities higher into the zone. This setup is also suggesting to me that the retest of the DP (which is 7b) is only likely to be a decent FTR if price has dropped through some strong levels before it returns up to the FTR (I know this is a central teaching of RTM, but this is me now seeing why for myself). If it does not do this, and makes a move back up towards the FTR/meat of the zone, then we should expect price to engulf the FTR upwards, and then turn deeper into the zone. This is another reason the stop should remain above the xone and not be moved to BE until something major is engulfed to the downside.

Also, to the left I have marked some 'kind of' compression. There is some fresh demand in there which 7a and 7b have to fight through, but once price moves up to 7c, it's a clearer path down.

Note the compression leading up to 7b and the LQ/FO sucking in the breakout traders to go long. A consolidation below a level suggests that the level will be broken, so it's important to be able to differentiate CP from simple flat price oscillation (that's what a base is, I guess) and a sinking bull flag or you may be going short at a developing RBR, not an imminent drop. So, we want to see HHs and HLs as we approach a supply zone, if price looks like it's ranging below the zone.

The Blue line at 7a shows the extreme high of the reaction at 7c. When price gets up to 7c, it has already tested the H1 DP to move down at 7a, so we should "expect" it to now move deeper into the zone, and as it has made some nice engulfs downwards, and been away for some time, we can "expect" to now have a more substantial reaction. But where? Well, the extreme high seems to go to the edge of a CP PAZ at 7a (but I haven't focussed on those, yet) but easier to spot is the QM it has made at 7c. The red circle shows why you don't trail your stop near BE, and in fact, you may want to place a short right there.

In this case, the FTR created by the RBD that is 9a has a very strong move away, making it a good candidate for a FTB short, but where should we expect the short to happen? Once more, the the test of the DP to go lower is an FTR in its own right, but right now, I'm picking my FTRs from the H1, and using the M5 for entries. If I pick FTRs off the M5, they are likely to be killed by the H1 action (or at least, it seems that way).

In the case of 9b we get the fantastic combo of some CP into the zone and a LQ spike right to the top edge of the zone, which forms a near perfect pin bar. Ooh, that's sexy.

There can be a LOT of material to wade through in public forums. I have read through this thread, and although there are lots of good posts, some of them caught my eye more than others. What follows is just a little summary of posts/info/charts I liked while flicking through and for those that may not have the time to read this forum end to end, could serve as a useful summary.

Whiteout: Every RBD/DBR or RBR/DBD is a decision point.

Whiteout: Decision points are a change in value. The bigger the change, the bigger the value.

Benhur: Nice chart showing how to correctly draw a base.

IF: Every DBR and RBD has its own importance and value, and nearly every one can be traded. For each one that you find, zoom out to the HTFs and see what historical significance the decision point has.

> Perhaps it's a failure to get back into an important PA Zone - these ones are special.

> Perhaps it's within an HTF compression zone to the left - ask yourself would you take this trade, or wait for the tip of the zone?

> The bigger picture will always help you decide on the significance of a DBR/RBD.

Tyoon: What defines a base is that price moves up or down, bases (consolidates, congests, clusters, etc.) then moves again either up or down. Here are the variations.

The standard DBD and RBR then the RBR and DBD then RBD during downtrend and DBR during uptrend.

Hopefully this could give you a better understanding. However as you have alluded to, H/L or S/R levels are almost always an intrinsic part to the development of any base. If you can find the levels responsible for the bases it can give you a much holistic picture on the chart.

IF: The two charts on the right, in HTF, can often look just like the two charts on the left. It's worth looking into these on your charts, and finding out which tend to perform better on price return - drop/consolidation/drops or drop/RBD/Drops, and the same for rallies.

Mel: I like Mel’s charts and explanations. I had to add at least one.

IF: IF asks this… but I am not sure what IF is pointing out? If someone knows, please post your thoughts...

IF: Pointing out the significance of the engulf.

Benhur: I thought this was an interesting comment about the lack on convincing buying/demand.

Rufus: To me how price leaves a zone is the way I judge it the most. Another is when the zone was formed and when price returns.

Benhur: Look for DBR/RDB that are the strongest. You can define strong level by 2 criteria:

1. How strong was the away move >> then >> it’s a strong level.

Why: We assume that at the decision point of breaking the balance (among sellers and buyers) are left with stacks of un-filled orders.

2. How Long was the Price at the defined level before it unbalanced > the least is better.

Why: As more time given for buyers and seller to negotiate, the more deals the close. The least amount of time they have to negotiate, we assume the more un-filled orders left at the zone.

IF: One thing which I have mentioned many times before, but not yet in Markepedia (soon to be remedied), is that in a bigger picture range, Supply and Demand zones near the edges may not hold as well as others. Fakeout often occur, because price is attracted to the limits of the range.

Benhur: Nothing promises that zone will hold price, even at first visit. The zones we mark on the charts are mainly a mapping of decisions in the market. Decision can take price either way. Zones are meant to be broken, and this market decision has its own significance too. As further you go with your reading skills, you will be able read the hints and clues for zones to hold or to break. Your task at this time, is to train your eyes defining the zones.Your next step, is to investigate how price is behaving around these zones. There are few things you should bare in mind while you do this work:

1. Be aware of how price had printed the zone you marked, what it was reacting to, and how the decision of price to move further look like.

2. Be aware of how price is approaching the Zones, what is the dynamic.

3. Is price come from a valid opposite zone? Remember that price goes from Demand to Supply and vice versa.

4. Be aware of the reaction of the first touch, how deep it went inside, what had stopped it if any?

5. What are higher or lower TF tell you. SD discipline is a Multi time frame concept. We trade price levels, not candles, so Story may vary on different TF.

6. (More Advanced) Look for correlations with Index and other pairs.

It might look intimidating, but actually it's should be very simple. Zones are always a reaction of past Price Action (aka: always look left). As much as you can go back in history, the better you understand be of how price move. There is no randomness for this market, all can be explained with PA reaction, result, decision. Just look for reasoning for levels and zones creation.

Looking back at my reply to your post, I realise that I did not answer the second part of your question, which was...

If this is a strong buy area, which TF do u suggest i look for PA to buy? H1/M15?

Unfortunately, there is no black & white (right or wrong) answer to this question. It depends on your trading experience, your trading time frames and personal style.

I would answer it by suggesting this...

Your should go down time frames until you can clearly identify the decision point that you are expecting to trade a reaction from. If you can see this on a 1 hr chart, than that is suitable. If you can see this on a 15 min chart, than that is suitable. However, the lower the time frame you can pinpoint a decision on, the lower your risk level. In saying that though, lower time frames generally require more time and higher skills.

There are many great RTM traders that trade from 4 hr and 1 hr candles, for example. But, you also have traders like IF that can identify decision points and hence entries on the 1 min chart. I recall a post where a RTM Master was saying that if they cannot identify a clear decision point on the 1 min chart, they will not enter.

Just go down to the time frame that allows you to clearly define your entry and risk. If you zoom down and cannot find this, consider skipping the trade. Instead, see where it reacted and then go down to the lower time frames and try to understand why price reacted where it did. It's better than taking a trade your are not 100% sure about, and you will speed up your learning doing this.

That's about the best answer I can give.

IFalso says that the best advice he can give you is not to read anything into candles themselves.

Hi Gian

To understand how to define a SD zone, we must understand what is behind the zone in terms of Order Flow. We expect that the inner boundary of the zone to be the price where remaining stacks of orders are waiting for execution. Since all we have is the chart, we can spot it by a closer look at the candles. There we look where was the last trade before one side overcome the other. pin bar is more like this

Characteristics of the Pin Bar Formation

• The pin bar should have a long upper or lower tail…the tail is also sometimes called the “wick” or the “shadow”…they all mean the same thing. It’s the “pointy” part of the pin bar that literally looks like a “tail” and that shows rejection or false break of a level.

• The area between the open and close of the pin bar is called the “body” or “real body”. It is typically colored white or another light color when the close was higher than the open and black or another dark color when the close was lower than the open.

• The open and close of the pin bar should be very close together or equal (same price), the closer the better.

• The open and close of the pin bar are near one end of the bar, the closer to the end the better.

• The shadow or tail of the pin bar sticks out (protrudes) from the surrounding price bars, the longer the tail of the pin bar the better.

• A general “rule of thumb” is that you want to see the pin bar tail be two/thirds the total pin bar length or more and the rest of the pin bar should be one/third the total pin bar length or less.

• The end opposite the tail is sometimes referred to as the “nose”

9. FTB of FTR formed at 7th point

10. Price engulfs previous high, however Flags right after it creating a Cap. Flag suggests the end of momentum. Therefore we cannot expect price to go much higher

Hi RTM! First of all, this is a wonderful experience for me to be with you here and learn all this awesome stuff. Next is my HW about caps on price. I used random charts and random segments of them - different TFs. It is really important for me (and my trading) to be as consistent as possible, so here are my rules how I marked rectangles. According to my understanding (mostly coming from the IFs video about the caps) I marked the most important ones, which I identified by liquidity gaps in them. First edge is of course high/low of the cap, but the second edge is open of the last green candle before drop in RBDs and open of the last red candle before the rally in DBR - that is according to my observations the most precise place, where the decision was made to turn the price (IMHO). (If there is no prior candle of different color befor price goes away i marked whole candle in base of the move).

note: it really depends on how the rectangle is placed. Sometimes price bounce from the very edges of the base, sometimes from the edge of liquidity gap, but mostly, when I don't want rectangles to be too big, rule above can be applied.

note2: red rectangles don't have reaction if I consider both edges of the rectangle. Price react to them though, but not precisely.

note3: it is obvious that RBD/DBR that are reactions to previous caps are much less important to future visits of price (and it was confirmed by IF and others all over the place ), however price tends to bounce from them too.

note4: because I really like statistics, here are the results from 87 reactions to caps -just for fun, of course: 67 was ok for scalp at least, 4 was fine to trade after they break and 16 was bad. Its 77% success rate
